newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish politicians ignoring 'real issues'-economists.
newsitem.headline: Irish politicians ignoring 'real issues'-economists.

text.p: Irish politicians are ignoring Ireland's "real economic issues" such as prospects for entering a single EU currency while touting imprudent give-away policies in the run-up to June 6 elections, economists said on Tuesday.

"They are all talking about tax reductions and welfare issues when we have a real potential crisis in the foreign exchange market which they are all ignoring," one leading economist, who asked not be named, said.
The Irish pound has plunged 10 pfennigs against the mark in the last month on speculation that Ireland will enter EMU at the European Exchange Rate Mechanism's (ERM) central rate.

"The key issue is, if we go into EMU, will we go in at our central rate of 2.41 marks. Unless the market is disabused of that notion we are going to drop another 15 pfennigs over the next 18 months,' Riada stockbrokers economist Dan McLaughlin said.
"This is obviously significantly inflationary but no-one is addressing this extremely pertinent foreign exchange issue."
Instead, he said, politicians appear to be quite unaware of the seriousness of the situation.

Economists argue that foreign investors are already concerned by what they call Ireland's "loose" fiscal policy and lack of attention to maintaining low inflation in the run-in to European Monetary Union (EMU), a goal all parties espouse as essential.

"Ireland has a booming economy, a falling currency and interest rates which, if EMU goes ahead, will presumably fall. Against that background it has strong asset price inflation and the correct policy response to that is to tighten fiscal policy," another economist said.
"Instead we have expansionary policies and there is no recognition in any of the political mandates that we might have to tighten fiscal policy."

Fine Gael leader John Bruton's centre-left coalition, which includes the Labour party and Democratic Left, indulged in a tax-give-away budget in January, hoping to ride into the current election on a wave of goodwill it engendered.

Both the ruling coalition and its main opposition, Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail party and ally, Mary Harney's Progressive Democrats, have broadly earmarked 1.5 billion punts for tax reductions over the next five years, if elected.

"At this stage of the economic cycle we should be running a budget surplus and not a deficit of 1.5 percent of GDP. The exchequer should not be borrowing it should be using this growth to cushion future shocks to the economy, particularly if we enter EMU without Britain," Bank of Ireland Group Treasury economist Jim Power said.
Power said if sterling misbehaves when Ireland is trapped inside a single currency, now is the time to build up the fiscal leeway to respond to that.

"In a post-EMU world the scope we have if the economy suffers an asymmetric shock is limited on the fiscal side and how limited that is depends on how prudent fiscal management will be over the next couple of years," Power said.
"Obviously if we are in surplus we will have a lot more flexibility."
